raw_case_text:
A 40-year-old male of Chinese ethnicity received allogeneic filgastrim-mobilised peripheral blood HSCT from his HLA 6/6 matched sister using reduced-intensity conditioning regimen. He was in his first complete remission from underlying B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia that had been diagnosed 6 months earlier. The course of transplantation was complicated by steroid-refractory grade III acute GVHD of the liver that began 7 months post-transplantation, requiring intensive immunosuppressive therapy with prednisolone followed by subsequent addition of other immunosuppressive agents including tacrolimus, mycopheolate mofetil and sirolimus for steroid-sparing purposes. He continued to receive dapsone and acyclovir prophylaxis, but was not on any antifungal prophylaxis.
In December 2007, at 9 months post-transplantation, he presented with acute-onset dry cough and shortness of breath following close contact with a client who had an upper respiratory tract infection (URTI). The initial chest X-ray was unremarkable with no evidence of pneumonia. His symptoms worsened over the ensuing few days, culminating one week later in acute respiratory failure requiring hospitalization and non-invasive mechanical ventilation in the intensive care unit (ICU). The patient was afebrile, with bilateral respiratory rhonchi on chest auscultation. Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts, renal and liver function. A chest x-ray (Figure 1) showed patchy bilateral lower zone and right upper zone air-space changes.
High resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the thorax (Figure 2) showed bilateral extensive, circumscribed areas of ground-glass opacification throughout both lung fields associated with a fine reticular pattern in keeping with pneumonitis. There were no nodules or pleural-based lesions to suggest a concomitant invasive fungal infection. Empirical antimicrobial therapy with intravenous levofloxacin and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was prescribed for community-acquired bacterial pneumonia and possible pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonitis. Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) was added as the possibility of influenza-associated pneumonia was entertained.
All microscopy and cultures of clinical samples were negative for aerobic bacteria, acid-fast bacilli or fungi. Reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reactions (PCR) performed on nasopharyngeal specimens were positive for RSV, although viral culture from the same swab was negative. Serial serum galactomannan screening and quantitative real-time PCR for cytomegalovirus DNA from peripheral blood were all negative. Diagnostic bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was not performed at this point owing to the concern of worsening hypoxemia.
The patient's overall condition improved gradually over one week, with reduced oxygen requirement and dyspnea. However, a repeat HRCT thorax (Figure 3) 4 weeks later showed new cavitary lesions. Nonetheless, a conservative approach of close clinical monitoring and radiological follow-up was adopted as the serial serum galactomannan tests remained negative and the patient's overall clinical condition continued to improve. He was discharged one week following the second HRCT.
However, he was re-admitted 10 days later with acute onset right pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea and diaphoresis. Chest x-ray (Figure 4A) and CT thorax (Figure 4B) showed enlarged thick-walled cavitary lesions in both lungs, with a moderate-sized right pneumothorax. Following chest tube insertion, he was transferred to the ICU for invasive mechanical ventilation. Thoracotomy with right upper lobectomy was subsequently performed. The histology was consistent with IPA, while lung tissue cultures grew Aspergillus fumigatus. He was prescribed voriconazole, which was continued for 6 months. Serial CT thorax showed gradual regression of the left pulmonary cavitary lesion and complete resolution of the ground grass changes. His respiratory symptoms improved despite receiving continued immunosuppressive therapy for his ongoing extensive chronic GVHD.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old Chinese male 9 months post-allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant presented with acute-onset dry cough and shortness of breath progressing to acute respiratory failure, followed 5 weeks later by acute right pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and diaphoresis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Nine months after an HLA-matched sibling allogeneic HSCT for B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (complicated by steroid-refractory grade III hepatic GVHD treated with prednisolone, tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and sirolimus without antifungal prophylaxis), the patient developed acute dry cough and dyspnea after close contact with an individual with an upper respiratory tract infection (December 2007). Within 1 week, he progressed to hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring ICU non-invasive ventilation for RSV pneumonitis. Although he clinically improved over 1 week and was discharged despite new asymptomatic cavitary lung lesions on 4-week follow-up HRCT, he was readmitted 10 days post-discharge with acute right pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and diaphoresis due to a secondary right pneumothorax.
subjective.past_medical_history: B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia in first complete remission status post reduced-intensity allogeneic peripheral blood HSCT from an HLA 6/6-matched sister 9 months prior; steroid-refractory grade III acute/extensive chronic hepatic GVHD on prednisolone, tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and sirolimus; receiving dapsone and acyclovir prophylaxis (no mould-active prophylaxis).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive initially for acute dry cough and progressive dyspnea (afebrile), and on readmission for acute right pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and diaphoresis.

objective.physical_examination: During initial ICU admission, the patient was afebrile in acute respiratory failure with bilateral rhonchi on chest auscultation.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine CBC, renal function, and liver function tests were normal. Initial chest X-ray was normal on day 1 but progressed at 1 week to patchy bilateral lower-zone and right upper-zone airspace opacities. Nasopharyngeal RT-PCR was positive for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Routine bacterial, AFB, and fungal smears/cultures and blood CMV quantitative PCR were negative. On readmission 5 weeks later, chest X-ray showed enlarged bilateral cavitary lesions and a moderate right pneumothorax.
objective.advanced_workup: Serial serum galactomannan assays remained persistently negative throughout both admissions. Initial thoracic HRCT showed extensive bilateral ground-glass opacities with a fine reticular pattern consistent with viral pneumonitis without nodules. Repeat HRCT 4 weeks later revealed new cavitary lung lesions, and readmission CT thorax 10 days post-discharge demonstrated enlarged thick-walled bilateral cavitary lesions complicated by a moderate right pneumothorax. Following chest tube drainage and right thoracotomy with right upper lobectomy, lung histopathology confirmed invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA) and lung tissue culture grew Aspergillus fumigatus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Proven cavitary invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (Aspergillus fumigatus) complicated by secondary right pneumothorax following severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) pneumonitis in a heavily immunosuppressed allogeneic HSCT recipient with chronic GVHD, confirmed by right upper lobectomy histopathology and lung tissue culture growing A. fumigatus despite persistently negative serial serum galactomannan assays. Treated with tube thoracostomy, invasive mechanical ventilation, right upper lobectomy, and a 6-month course of voriconazole, resulting in gradual regression of the contralateral left cavitary lesion, complete resolution of ground-glass opacities, and sustained respiratory recovery despite ongoing immunosuppression for chronic GVHD.
